author: David Friedman Sports Columnist
title: Let me introduce you to my dad - NewsBreak
text: This Sunday is Father’s Day. I thought I might use the opportunity to talk about my Dad a little bit. He grew up in New York, an only child and son to a World War II veteran turned businessman and an adoring mother and wife. My Dad’s Dad was tough, but genuinely cared. It was a different time and Grandpa articulated his feelings about as well as most men did back then, which is to say not very well. It didn’t mean he loved his family any less. He worked hard to provide not only for them, but his community where he was heavily involved in both local and national politics. There are pictures of Grandpa with Jimmy Carter. My grandmother may have been the sweetest woman I’ve ever met. I was her youngest grandchild and that perspective may have provided a rose colored tint to my memories of her, but I’m certain she never uttered a cross word in her life. Grandma was absolutely lovely and, surprisingly, a fan of kickboxing. Grandpa boxed so I see how he landed her. Like everyone else, my father was a product of not only his environment but his era. It was the day after his 16th birthday when the first wave of U.S. troops went into South Vietnam. My Dad, recognizing that going to Vietnam was an inevitability, enlisted in the Air Force after graduation. He was one of the fortunate ones to come back home, but nobody came back from Vietnam the same person that left and he was no exception. He still won’t talk about his time there and I no longer ask. He was stationed at Seymour Johnson AFB when he met my Mom working at the NCO Club on base. She was a ginger divorced mother of two boys from North Carolina and he was a Jewish “yankee” bachelor. He was and is lucky to have her but I applaud anyone who voluntarily becomes a parent to two kids. They married and, while my brothers have a father, they call mine Dad to this day. I showed up a few years later and my father eventually retired from the Air Force before working another career worth of jobs. Those included videotape delivery, assisting mentally and physically handicapped adults with job and life training, as well as my least favorite job of his, prison guard. He did what my Mom and countless other parents have also done to provide their family, myself included. He did whatever needed to be done. My Dad was and is his own version of a tough military Dad however, unlike his father, mine hugs me every time he seems me and reminds me that he loves me. Every good parent wants better for their children than they had and he does his part with my brothers and I, as we will never have to question if our Dad loves or supports us. My Dad is far from perfect (so is my son’s Dad) but I’m incredibly lucky to have him. I too want better for my son than I had but credit to my Dad, he set the bar pretty high. Happy Father’s Day to my Dad, to my best friend and one of the best Dads I know, and to your Dad too. Subscribe to The Enterprise
